Managing with ai task 1 
Pepijn Fermont 
16-09-2026 
  

Task 1: 
The prompt i will use: 
Role 
 You are an AI research analyst supporting an industrial organization that wants to 
reduce operational complexity, improve energy efficiency, and investigate intelligent 
automation in a high-stakes industrial environment, specifically steelmaking and 
furnace scheduling. 
Context 
 I will provide you with a set of documents that were collected by a former engineer. The 
archive contains potentially valuable knowledge, but the information is fragmented, 
inconsistent, and scattered across different documents. 
This is Task 1: Inventory & Initial Scan. The purpose is not yet to produce final 
recommendations, but to create a reliable overview of the available knowledge and 
determine the boundaries of the knowledge domain. 
Task 
 Analyse every document in the provided Document Set and perform the following 
steps: 
1. Document inventory 
 Create a complete inventory of all documents. For each document extract, 
where available:  
a. File name / document ID  
b. Title  
c. Author(s)  
d. Organization or institution  
e. Publication/source  
f. Publication date  
g. Document type (academic paper, report, technical document, 
presentation, manual, etc.)  
h. Keywords  
i. Main topic  
j. A short 2–4 sentence summary  
k. One or two representative snippets or passages that indicate what the 
document is about  
2. Initial relevance scan 
 For each document, identify which of the following themes it relates to:  
a. Steelmaking  

b. Furnace operations  
c. Production/furnace scheduling  
d. Operational complexity  
e. Energy efficiency / energy consumption  
f. Optimization  
g. Artificial intelligence / machine learning  
h. Intelligent automation  
i. Decision support  
j. Industrial safety / reliability  
k. Other relevant themes discovered in the documents  
Do not rank documents as “good” or “bad”. Instead, briefly explain their apparent 
relevance to the project. 
3. Knowledge-domain boundaries 
 Based only on the supplied documents, determine the apparent boundaries of 
the knowledge domain. Identify:  
a. The main subjects covered  
b. Important subdomains  
c. Technologies and methods mentioned  
d. Industrial processes covered  
e. What appears to be inside the scope of the archive  
f. What appears to be outside or insufficiently covered  
g. Major gaps or missing information that may need further research  
4. Initial organizational synthesis 
 Group related documents into logical thematic clusters. For every cluster:  
a. Give the cluster a descriptive name  
b. List the documents belonging to it  
c. Explain what type of knowledge the cluster contains  
d. Identify connections with other clusters  
5. Terminology scan 
 Identify recurring technical concepts, abbreviations, methods, systems, 
equipment, algorithms, and industrial terminology. Create a short glossary for 
terminology that is important for understanding the archive.  
6. Tools and analytical approach 
 Briefly state which analytical methods are appropriate for processing this 
archive in later stages, such as:  
a. Metadata extraction  
b. Semantic document clustering  
c. Keyword extraction  
d. Entity extraction  

e. Cross-document comparison  
f. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)  
g. Knowledge graphs  
h. Other suitable GenAI/NLP methods  
Explain briefly what each proposed method could contribute. Do not yet implement 
methods that require information beyond the provided documents. 
Required output 
Start with a table containing the document inventory: 
ID Document Author(s) Date Type Keywords Main 
topic 
Relevant 
themes 
Short 
summary 
Then provide the following sections: 
1. Overview of the Document Set 
 Give a concise description of the archive and the types of knowledge it contains. 
2. Knowledge Domain and Boundaries 
 Describe the domain, subdomains and scope. 
3. Thematic Clusters 
 Organize the documents into logical groups and explain the relationships between 
them. 
4. Important Terminology 
 Provide the glossary. 
5. Knowledge Gaps and Uncertainties 
 Explain what information appears to be missing, contradictory or insufficient. 
6. Proposed Tools for Further Analysis 
 Explain which AI/NLP/GenAI tools would be useful in the next stages and why. 
7. Initial Conclusion 
 Give a concise synthesis of what the archive currently tells us about reducing 
operational complexity, improving energy efficiency and deploying intelligent 
automation in steelmaking/furnace scheduling. 
Important rules 
• Base every statement on the supplied documents.  
• Do not invent missing metadata.  

• If information is unavailable, write “Not identified”.  
• Clearly distinguish information stated explicitly in a document from your own 
interpretation.  
• Mention the source document whenever making an important factual claim.  
• Preserve technical terminology used in the original documents.  
• Identify contradictions between documents rather than silently resolving them.  
• At this stage, prioritize inventory, structure and scope definition over detailed 
recommendations.  
• Analyse all supplied documents, not only the most relevant ones.

1 Overview of the Document Set
The archive contains 31 research documents totaling 456 PDF pages. It is predominantly academic: 24 journal articles or case studies, six conference papers or proceedings contributions, and one perspective article. Publication dates run from 2016 to 2026, with most documents published from 2020 onward.
The core of the set is energy-aware production scheduling in steel and heat-intensive manufacturing. Direct steel topics include steelmaking-continuous casting, hot rolling, hot-strip mills, reheating and heat-treatment furnaces, hot-metal ladles, EAF scheduling, by-product gas systems, off-spec product reallocation and cold-strip rolling [D01-D03, D07, D09-D12, D14-D15, D17-D19, D22-D24, D26, D28]. Adjacent cases cover forging, casting, steel-powder production, aluminum rolling and generic job shops [D08, D13, D16, D20-D21, D27, D29-D31].
Methodologically, the archive combines mathematical programming and operational research with evolutionary algorithms, robust and stochastic methods, time-series forecasting, simulation, digital twins, deep reinforcement learning and explainable AI. Several documents use real plant data or industrial cases, but the evidence is heterogeneous: objectives, system boundaries, uncertainty assumptions and reported metrics differ substantially across papers.
2 Knowledge Domain and Boundaries
The apparent knowledge domain is the design of data-informed and optimization-based planning, scheduling and control for steel production and related heat-intensive processes. The archive treats operational complexity as a combination of tightly coupled production stages, limited resources, product-specific constraints, uncertainty, disruptions, energy-system interactions and the need for fast decisions [D02-D03, D09-D12, D17-D18, D23-D24, D28].
Main Subjects and Subdomains
Furnace and thermal-process scheduling: idle energy, batching, sequencing, parallel furnaces, residence time, deterioration, no-wait and no-idle constraints [D01, D07, D10, D14-D15, D17, D22-D23, D27-D31].
Steel plant and inter-stage coordination: steelmaking-continuous casting, ladle dispatching, ironmaking-steelmaking interfaces, hot-strip rolling and product reallocation [D03, D11-D12, D17-D18, D26, D28].
Industrial energy systems: electricity-market response, renewable uncertainty, multi-energy media and by-product gas balancing [D05, D09, D21, D24].
Digital and intelligent production: digital twins, IoT integration, live scheduling, DRL, MARL, LLM-assisted reward design and agent-based architectures [D05, D09-D11, D13, D16, D18-D21, D23, D26, D30].
Human and governance dimensions: XAI, counterfactual explanations, trustworthy AI, operator feedback, human-centric Industry 5.0 and process safety [D04, D06, D08, D13, D16, D20, D25].
Processes and Equipment Covered
The archive covers electric vacuum hardening furnaces [D01], soaking and heat-treatment furnaces [D07, D22, D27], walking-beam and other reheating furnaces [D10, D14-D15, D17, D23, D28], EAF-based steelmaking [D09], converters and continuous casting through SCC models [D03, D12, D18], hot-strip and hot-rolling lines [D02, D17, D26, D28], cold rolling [D19], hot-metal ladles [D12, D18], and by-product gas production, storage and consumption [D24]. Adjacent manufacturing coverage includes casting, forging, steel powder, aluminum cold rolling and generic job shops [D13, D16, D20-D21, D27, D29-D31].
Inside the Apparent Scope
Short-term and online production scheduling, rescheduling and dispatching.
Energy-aware objectives including consumption, cost, idle energy, demand response, gas utilization and flare reduction.
Multi-objective trade-offs involving makespan, tardiness, quality penalties, robustness, stability and energy.
Algorithmic and digital support for dynamic decisions, including industrial prototypes and plant-data case studies.
Explainability, human oversight and safety as enabling conditions for intelligent automation.
Outside or Insufficiently Covered
Long-term production-network design, raw-material procurement, sales and order promising, workforce planning beyond one human-centric job-shop study, and maintenance optimization as a primary topic.
Detailed furnace combustion, refractory degradation, emissions chemistry and metallurgical quality models; most furnace papers abstract these into processing times, energy functions or empirical predictors.
A full end-to-end integrated steelworks model spanning raw materials, ironmaking, steelmaking, casting, rolling, finishing, utilities and logistics.
Cybersecurity, data governance, model lifecycle management, sensor validation, fail-safe fallback and regulatory assurance for autonomous industrial AI.
Standardized economic evidence such as implementation cost, payback, staffing impact and sustained post-deployment KPI performance.
3 Thematic Clusters
4 Important Terminology
5 Knowledge Gaps and Uncertainties
No common baseline or KPI dictionary. Energy is expressed as idle-energy functions, GJ per tonne, energy cost, operating time, demand-response reward, gas flaring or percentage savings. Reported improvements therefore cannot be compared directly [D01, D09, D12, D14-D15, D22, D24, D27, D31].
Industrial validation varies from numerical experiments and literature cases to plant data, virtual plants and open-loop prototypes. The archive rarely reports sustained closed-loop deployment, operator override rates or long-term drift [D10-D11, D14, D19, D27, D30].
Data requirements are incomplete. Papers identify historical process data, live sensor status or forecasts, but usually do not define data quality thresholds, missing-data handling, lineage, ownership or integration effort [D03, D10, D14, D19, D24, D30].
Safety evidence is thin relative to automation ambition. D25 argues for intelligence augmentation and human involvement, while many scheduling papers evaluate optimality and computational performance without hazard analysis, fail-safe behavior or validation under abnormal plant states [D05, D09-D10, D18, D20-D21, D23, D30].
Furnace physics and metallurgical quality are only partly coupled to schedules. D01 uses a dynamic furnace model and D14 predicts energy, but most scheduling models simplify thermal state, combustion, refractory condition and material-quality consequences [D07, D15, D17, D22-D23, D27-D29].
The archive does not contain a complete end-to-end steelworks ontology or integrated reference architecture connecting production, energy, maintenance, quality, logistics and human decisions.
Economic and organizational adoption evidence is limited. XAI, user trust and human-centricity are discussed [D04, D06, D13, D16, D25], but cost of implementation, change management, training and accountability are not quantified.
Cybersecurity and adversarial robustness are insufficiently covered. D10 mentions digital-twin security literature, but the archive contains no dedicated treatment of industrial network security, access control, attack detection or secure fallback.
Methodological Tensions and Contradictions
The documents do not present one consistent answer to idle operation. D31 removes idle time as the green constraint, whereas D01 explicitly models necessary idle periods and optimizes their continuous furnace dynamics. These approaches apply to different equipment assumptions and should not be merged without checking furnace thermal constraints.
The archive also contains a tension between autonomous real-time decision making and human oversight. DRL and agent papers emphasize speed and adaptive control [D05, D09-D11, D18, D20-D21, D30], while D06, D13, D16 and D25 make explanation, human feedback or intelligence augmentation part of the system requirement. The documents do not resolve where final authority should sit in a high-stakes steel plant.
Optimization models differ in uncertainty treatment. Some assume deterministic processing and prove exact or optimal algorithms for the stated model [D01, D23, D31], while others explicitly model stochastic breakdowns, uncertain arrivals, prices, renewable output or rolling times [D02-D03, D07, D09, D24, D28]. Their performance claims are valid under different information assumptions and are not directly interchangeable.
There is one metadata ambiguity: D02 was published online in 2017 but appears in a 2019 journal volume. Both dates are retained rather than silently selecting one.
6 Proposed Tools for Further Analysis
7 Initial Conclusion
The archive supports a coherent initial hypothesis: operational complexity and energy use in steel production can be reduced by coordinating decisions across time, equipment and process boundaries rather than optimizing isolated machines. The strongest direct examples integrate furnace control with scheduling [D01], reheating with rolling [D17], production with ladle dispatching [D12], and energy supply with plant operation [D05, D09, D24].
Energy efficiency is treated mainly as a scheduling and coordination problem. The mechanisms include reducing avoidable idle or residence time, selecting batches and sequences, exploiting time-varying electricity prices, balancing plant energy media, limiting flaring and coordinating thermal processes with downstream capacity [D01, D07, D09, D15, D22-D24, D27-D31]. The archive does not establish a single best method because the models use different process boundaries and KPIs.
Intelligent automation appears in three layers: prediction and forecasting, optimization and learned decision policies, and live digital representations. Forecasts and ML estimate arrivals, energy or rolling force [D03, D14, D19, D24]; mathematical and evolutionary methods generate schedules [D01-D03, D07-D08, D12, D15, D17-D18, D22-D23, D26-D31]; DRL, multi-agent systems and digital twins support adaptive or live decisions [D05, D09-D11, D13, D16, D18-D21, D26, D30].
For a high-stakes industrial environment, the archive also sets a clear boundary: computational performance alone is insufficient. Explainability, human oversight, safety, data quality, fail-safe behavior and evidence from sustained deployment remain underdeveloped relative to the proposed autonomy [D04, D06, D08, D13, D16, D25]. The next stage should therefore build a traceable evidence matrix and knowledge graph before selecting technologies or making implementation recommendations.

Term | Meaning in this archive
SCC | Steelmaking-continuous casting; a coupled production chain modeled as a hybrid flow shop in D03 and D12.
HSM | Hot strip mill; the roughing and finishing stages that roll reheated slabs into strip [D24, D28].
SRRF | Steel rolling reheating furnace; the furnace whose heat energy per tonne is predicted in D14.
EAF | Electric arc furnace; electricity-intensive batch steelmaking equipment used in the demand-response case in D09.
PPC and PPS | Production planning and control; production planning and scheduling. D13 uses PPC and D16 uses PPS.
JSSP | Job-shop scheduling problem; an NP-hard sequencing and allocation problem used in D08 and D20.
IPPS | Integrated process planning and scheduling; process routes and schedules are chosen together [D30].
MILP | Mixed-integer linear programming; an exact optimization formulation used throughout the archive, including D09, D12, D22, D24 and D31.
Makespan | Completion time of the full job set; a common production-efficiency objective [D15, D16, D29, D31].
Tardiness | Delay beyond a due date, sometimes weighted across jobs; paired with energy in D07 and D22.
Pareto front | The set of non-dominated trade-off solutions in a multi-objective problem [D02, D07-D08, D17, D22, D26].
No-wait and no-idle | No-wait prevents delay between successive job operations [D22]; no-idle prevents gaps on a machine [D31].
Deterioration effect | Processing or reheating time increases with waiting or position, often because slabs cool before reheating [D02, D23].
Robust optimization | Optimization against uncertain parameters or scenarios, used for release and processing-time uncertainty [D03, D28].
Chance-constrained programming | Constraints are required to hold with a specified probability; used in the release-time rescheduler in D03.
Rolling horizon | Forecast and optimize a finite future window, then update as new data arrive [D24].
GA and NSGA-II | Genetic algorithm; NSGA-II is a non-dominated sorting variant for multi-objective optimization [D02, D07-D08, D14, D26-D27, D31].
PSO and MOPSO | Particle swarm optimization and its multi-objective form [D26, D28].
GWO | Grey Wolf Optimizer; a population metaheuristic adapted to heating-furnace scheduling in D15.
DRL and MARL | Deep reinforcement learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning for learned sequential decisions [D05, D09, D13, D20-D21, D30].
MDP and POMDP | Markov decision process and partially observable MDP; state-action-reward models for sequential control under full or partial observability [D05, D09, D21].
SAC PPO DQN | Soft Actor-Critic, Proximal Policy Optimization and Deep-Q-Network; DRL algorithms appearing in D05, D09 and D30.
Digital twin | A live digital representation linked to physical assets and data, used for monitoring, simulation and optimization [D10, D16, D19, D26, D30].
XAI | Explainable artificial intelligence; methods that make model behavior and recommendations understandable [D04, D06, D08, D13].
Counterfactual explanation | An explanation describing small input or operational changes that would produce another outcome [D08].
Intelligence augmentation | AI that collaborates with and supports human operators instead of replacing them [D25].
Demand response | Adjustment of electricity use in response to prices or grid conditions [D09, D21, D27].
BFG COG and LDG | Blast-furnace gas, coke-oven gas and Linz-Donawitz gas; steelworks by-products scheduled in D24.
ALADIN | Augmented Lagrangian based Alternating Direction Inexact Newton method used for nonconvex steel-energy optimization in D05.
KAN | Kolmogorov-Arnold Network; the policy-network architecture used in the LLM-assisted DRL framework in D20.
Method | Contribution in later stages
Metadata extraction and normalization | Parse title pages, DOI, authors, affiliations, dates, venues and document type into a controlled schema; flag conflicts such as online versus issue dates.
Layout-aware OCR and document parsing | Preserve headings, equations, tables, figure captions and page references. This is necessary for scanned or extraction-resistant PDFs such as D26.
Keyword and keyphrase extraction | Build a consistent vocabulary across author keywords and full text, then map variants such as reheating furnace, heating furnace and heat-treatment furnace.
Entity and relation extraction | Identify equipment, process stages, energy media, objectives, constraints, datasets, algorithms, KPIs and reported results, including links such as algorithm-solves-problem.
Semantic document clustering | Use embeddings to test and refine the five manual clusters, expose bridge documents and identify isolated topics without imposing keyword-only groupings.
Cross-document evidence matrix | Compare process boundary, decision horizon, uncertainty, objectives, constraints, input data, method, baseline, reported outcome and deployment maturity for every paper.
Contradiction and assumption detection | Surface incompatible assumptions, metrics and control philosophies, such as no-idle versus optimized idle control or autonomous action versus human approval.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation | Create chunk-level retrieval with document and page citations so later questions can be answered from the archive without blending unsupported claims.
Knowledge graph | Connect process stages, equipment, energy flows, decisions, constraints, algorithms, KPIs and evidence. This would make missing interfaces and duplicated concepts visible.
Table and equation extraction | Capture objective functions, constraints, parameter definitions and numerical results for formal comparison rather than relying only on narrative summaries.
Human review workflow | Require engineering review for extracted constraints, safety-critical claims and mappings between academic models and plant terminology before operational use.
